title: Hardware Wallet Security Starts With the Supply Chain
summary: Hardware wallets protect private keys without exposing them to internet-connected devices or relying on an exchange to hold them.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


Hardware wallets protect private keys by keeping them offline, but their security also depends on the software, manufacturers, third-party services, and distribution channels surrounding them.


-


Incidents involving Ledger, Trezor, and Coldcard show how cryptographic flaws, fraudulent applications, customer data breaches, and device tampering can put assets and sensitive information at risk.


-


Hardware wallet owners can reduce exposure through verified software, careful recovery phrase management, security updates, and attention to manufacturer disclosures.


-


BitGo’s qualified custody offers an alternative to managing private keys independently, giving eligible individual investors access to regulated custody infrastructure and institutional security controls.


Hardware wallets protect private keys without exposing them to internet-connected devices or relying on an exchange to hold them. Keeping keys offline remains an effective safeguard, but recent security incidents have demonstrated the limitations of self-custody hardware wallets.


This year alone, cryptographic flaws have made private keys recoverable, fraudulent applications have stolen recovery phrases, and breaches at third-party providers have exposed customer information. In October, Ledger[reported](https://x.com/Ledger_Support/status/2108968264055345381) physical tampering involving devices sold through a reseller.


Together, these incidents show why hardware wallet security extends beyond the device itself. The protection of an individual’s funds relies on the entire supply chain behind the device. We have now seen how software, vendors, and distribution channels can all be a single point of failure.


## Are Hardware Wallets Safe?


Hardware wallets provide strong protection against attacks on internet-connected computers and phones. They store private keys in a dedicated offline device and sign transactions without exposing those keys to the connected computer. Many also display transaction details on their own screens, allowing owners to verify what they are approving.


These protections helped hardware wallets become a popular alternative to keeping cryptocurrency on exchanges. Following the collapse of Mt. Gox in 2014, self-custody attracted greater attention. Manufacturers introduced dedicated devices for securing private keys. For the last decade, this has been a standard of protection for smaller investors just getting started on their crypto journey.


In 2020, Kraken Security Labs demonstrated that attackers could[extract wallet seeds](https://www.theblock.co/post/54631/kraken-security-labs-hackers-can-exploit-trezor-hardware-wallets-with-only-15-minutes-of-physical-access-to-the-device) from certain Trezor devices through voltage glitching, an attack requiring physical access and specialized equipment. More recent incidents have exposed risks to other devices that physical security alone cannot prevent. Vulnerabilities in key generation, signing software, and connected applications can put funds at risk without attackers ever possessing the device, even while the hardware wallet remains offline and functions normally.


## Where Hardware Wallet Security Can Break Down


The risks surrounding hardware wallets have different causes and consequences. Some directly expose keys or recovery phrases. Others manipulate transaction approvals or expose customer information that attackers can use for phishing.


### Firmware and Cryptographic Vulnerabilities


Hardware wallets rely on software to generate private keys and authorize transactions. Vulnerabilities in either process can undermine offline storage.


In 2026, Zilliqa disclosed a[flaw in its Ledger application](https://www.zilliqa.com/ledger-incident/post-mortem/) that had existed since 2019. An error in how the application handled the randomness required for secure transaction signatures allowed attackers to reconstruct account private keys from multiple public signatures.


Zilliqa identified at least 6,772 exposed accounts, of which 51 were drained before legacy transactions were disabled in July 2026. The flaw affected the legacy Zilliqa signing path. It did not expose recovery phrases or compromise assets on other blockchains held through the same device.


A separate Coldcard vulnerability originated in a March 2021 firmware release. A build and integration error weakened the randomness used to generate wallet seeds, making some private keys easier to predict. Theft began in July 2026, with[preliminary estimates](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/the-largest-hardware-wallet-exploit-of-2026-inside-the-usd-116-million-coldcard-hack) putting losses at approximately 1,816 BTC, then worth $116 million.


Both incidents demonstrate how a wallet can remain offline while its protections fail. They also reveal a limitation of software updates: correcting a vulnerability does not restore the safety of keys already exposed. Affected owners may need to generate new keys and transfer their assets, even if they did “everything right”.


### Third-Party Vendors and Customer Data


Hardware wallet manufacturers rely on third parties for payments, shipping, and customer communications. These relationships introduce risks beyond the devices themselves.


Ledger experienced a major customer data breach in 2020. In January 2026, a separate[incident involving e-commerce partner Global-e](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/crypto-wallet-firm-ledger-faces-123240083.html) exposed customer contact information without compromising Ledger's wallet systems.


Trezor experienced two third-party incidents in 2026. A[breach involving shipping partner ShipMonk](https://trezor.io/blog/news/recent-customer-data-exposed-in-shipping-provider-incident) affected customer records, including information that should have been deleted under data retention arrangements. A September[breach involving email provider Brevo](https://trezor.io/blog/news/security-incident-at-brevo-our-third-party-email-provider) exposed 347,149 marketing contacts.


In October 2026, Keystone[disclosed](https://x.com/KeystoneWallet/status/2114719318722404578) that attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party website monitoring tool, exposing personal information associated with 25,964 customer purchase records and 12,873 incomplete checkout records. Keystone also acknowledged that failures in its automated deletion process had left some customer information stored beyond its 180-day retention policy.


These incidents did not directly compromise hardware wallets or recovery phrases. However, names, contact details, and purchase records can help attackers identify cryptocurrency owners and create convincing phishing messages. An attacker who persuades an owner into disclosing a recovery phrase can then gain control of the associated assets without exploiting the device or obtaining physical access.


### Fake Wallet Applications and Compromised Software


Hardware wallets typically rely on companion applications to display balances, construct transactions, and communicate with the device. Attackers can exploit these interfaces without compromising the hardware.


In April 2026, a[fraudulent Ledger Live application](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fake-ledger-live-app-on-apples-app-store-stole-95m-in-crypto/) appeared on Apple's App Store. Reporting attributed approximately $9.5 million in cryptocurrency losses across 50 victims to the fake macOS application. It used a fabricated version history to appear legitimate before asking users to enter their recovery phrases.


With those phrases, attackers could recreate the victims' wallets without possessing their devices.


Software connecting wallets to decentralized applications can also be compromised. In December 2023, attackers published malicious versions of[Ledger's Connect Kit](https://www.ledger.com/blog/security-incident-report) after compromising a former employee's software publishing account. Connected applications loaded the malicious library, which tricked users into signing transactions or approvals that drained assets.


Ledger reported approximately five hours between the initial compromise and complete resolution, with active draining concentrated in a shorter period.


These incidents illustrate different software risks. Fraudulent applications can steal recovery information, while compromised dependencies can manipulate what users approve through otherwise legitimate applications.


### Device Distribution and Supply Chain Risks


Hardware wallets pass through manufacturing, shipping, and distribution channels before reaching their owners. Manufacturers recommend purchasing through official sources and completing available authenticity checks. Ledger also acknowledges that its[Genuine Check](https://www.ledger.com/academy/topics/crypto/how-to-securely-buy-your-ledger-from-amazon-and-retailers) cannot detect every unauthorized physical modification.


In October 2026, Ledger investigated thefts involving devices purchased from CryptoBilis, a reseller serving Southeast Asian customers. That same month, Ledger asked the reseller to suspend sales.


According to[reporting on the investigation](https://www.coindesk.com/tech/2026/10/13/ledger-says-spy-chip-inside-cryptobilis-ledger-devices-transmitted-wallet-keys-over-mobile-network) , Ledger identified an unauthorized implant inside an affected device. The component captured recovery phrases as they appeared on the screen during setup and transmitted them over a cellular connection.


Ledger said the implant did not modify the secure element, operating system, transactions, or signatures. It captured recovery information when the device displayed it to the owner.


Onchain researchers estimated substantial losses, but Ledger has not yet confirmed the total value stolen or number of victims. The investigation into who modified the devices and where the tampering occurred remains ongoing.


The Keystone breach also exposed a separate weakness in device authentication. In its October 26[update](https://x.com/KeystoneWallet/status/2114719318722404578) , the company confirmed that attackers had obtained the key used to verify whether its hardware wallets were genuine. Although the key was not involved in generating private keys or signing transactions, its exposure could allow counterfeit devices to pass Keystone's authentication checks. Keystone said it would replace the key in newly manufactured devices and destroy 18,835 unshipped devices containing the compromised key.


The Ledger and Keystone incidents highlight different limitations of hardware wallet authenticity checks. Verifying genuine software or a secure element may not reveal unauthorized physical modifications, while a compromised authentication key can allow counterfeit devices to pass verification. Purchasing through established channels and completing manufacturer checks can reduce risk, but those safeguards depend on the integrity of the devices and systems behind them.


Regulatory expectations are also changing. Reporting obligations under the European Union's[Cyber Resilience Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cra-reporting) began on September 11, 2026, covering actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe security incidents affecting products with digital elements. Broader product cybersecurity obligations are scheduled for December 2027.


## How to Protect Your Crypto From Hardware Wallet Risks


Hardware wallet owners can reduce exposure by addressing the different ways devices and supporting systems can be compromised. The appropriate response depends on whether the threat involves physical tampering, malicious software, exposed customer information, or vulnerable keys.


Purchase devices through manufacturers or listed resellers, complete available authenticity checks during setup, and obtain companion applications and firmware through official sources. The fake Ledger Live incident shows why an app store listing alone does not establish authenticity.


Recovery phrases should remain offline and private. Never enter them into an unexpected application, website, or security verification request. Treat unsolicited security notices and recovery instructions carefully, particularly after a manufacturer or service provider discloses a breach. Accurate personal information does not prove that a message is legitimate.


If a cryptographic flaw has exposed a seed or private key, installing corrected software may leave existing assets at risk. Follow the manufacturer's guidance and, where required, transfer funds to a wallet controlled by securely generated replacement keys.


When authorizing transactions, compare recipient addresses and transaction details on the hardware wallet's screen with the intended transaction. This can help detect certain forms of manipulation, although it cannot protect against every software or signing vulnerability.


[Multi-signature arrangements](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/multisig-wallet-transactions/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=wallet_security_supply_chain) can also reduce dependence on a single private key, provided the keys are generated, stored, and managed independently. If one flaw compromises enough keys to meet the signing threshold, the wallet can still be vulnerable.


These practices reduce risk, but self-custody still requires owners to evaluate devices and software, protect recovery information, monitor disclosures, and respond when vulnerabilities threaten existing keys.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Can hardware wallets be hacked?


Yes. Vulnerabilities in firmware, cryptographic software, physical hardware, or connected applications can put assets at risk. Some attacks require physical access, while others exploit weak keys or signatures, steal recovery phrases, or trick users into approving harmful transactions.


### Are hardware wallets safer than exchanges?


Hardware wallets give investors direct control over their keys and reduce dependence on an exchange's custody arrangements. They also place responsibility for backups, updates, recovery information, and transaction verification on the owner. Security depends on the specific device, provider, custody arrangements, and investor practices.


### Can someone steal crypto from a hardware wallet without the device?


Yes. An attacker who obtains the recovery phrase can recreate the wallet and transfer assets without the original device. Certain cryptographic vulnerabilities can also make private keys recoverable through weak key generation or public transaction signatures.


### What is a hardware wallet supply chain attack?


A hardware wallet supply chain attack compromises a component, provider, or distribution channel involved in creating, delivering, or supporting a wallet. Examples include tampered devices and malicious software dependencies. Breaches at third-party providers can also expose customer information that enables subsequent phishing attacks.


### Is qualified custody safer than a hardware wallet?


[Qualified custody](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/qualified-custody-vs-self-custody/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=wallet_security_supply_chain) and self-custody address different risks. Hardware wallet owners control their keys and manage security themselves. Qualified custody places key management with a regulated provider that may offer additional operating controls, asset segregation, and applicable insurance. Customers rely on that provider to maintain those protections.


### How is qualified custody different from my favorite exchange?


When you leave crypto on an exchange, your assets may be exposed to the exchange's financial risks. If the exchange fails, you could be treated as an unsecured creditor. With BitGo, your assets are held at BitGo Bank & Trust, our federally regulated national trust bank, in segregated qualified custody structured to be bankruptcy-remote. Your crypto remains yours, separate from BitGo's corporate assets, with institutional-grade security.


### Is BitGo qualified custody really free for individual investors?


BitGo offers qualified custody to eligible individual investors with no custody fee. Trading, staking, and other services may have separate fees, eligibility requirements, or terms.
